{{Short description|Division of mathematical analysis}}
{{Unreferenced|date=August 2015}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''value distribution theory of holomorphic functions''' is a division of [[mathematical analysis]]. The purpose of the theory is to provide quantitative measures of the number of times a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] ''f''(''z'') assumes a [[Value (mathematics)|value]] ''a'', as ''z'' grows in size, refining the [[Picard theorem]] on behaviour close to an [[essential singularity]]. The theory exists for [[analytic function]]s (and [[meromorphic function]]s) of one complex variable ''z'', or of [[several complex variables]].

In the case of one variable, the term '''[[Nevanlinna theory]]''', after [[Rolf Nevanlinna]], is also common.  The now-classical theory received renewed interest when [[Paul Vojta]] suggested some analogies to the problem of integral solutions to [[Diophantine equation]]s.  These turned out to involve some close parallels and to lead to fresh points of view on the [[Mordell conjecture]] and related questions.
